sentiment.instructions: Judge the overall sentiment the author expresses in the text (tweet-style, any language). Focus on the author's own attitude or emotional tone toward the topic, event or people mentioned, not just whether the subject matter is good or bad news.

positive.description: The author conveys excitement, happiness, anticipation, praise, gratitude, admiration, amusement or approval, including upbeat news shared approvingly (wins, celebrations, birthdays, looking forward to an event). Mild enthusiasm or a pleased tone is enough.
examples: Not even 20 pages into Paper Towns and the book centers around the night of May 5th. I know its gonna be a good one now!

neutral.description: Mostly factual, informational or conversational: announcements, schedules, questions, reports, plans or observations without a clear positive or negative attitude, or with mixed, ironic or very weak feeling. Hypothetical worries or light jokes without real emotion also fit here.
examples: I may be sleep deprived but I promise you that some kid at Dunkin today looked like a sprout.

negative.description: The author conveys frustration, anger, sadness, disappointment, criticism, contempt, mockery, fear or hostility (including bigoted or insulting remarks), or complains about problems, failures, bad events, deaths or attacks. Sarcastic put-downs count as negative.
examples: The tragedy of only thinking up hilarious tweets for the Summer Olympics now is that in four years there may be no place for them.
